characters: Grandpa Mensah: a cheerful, dignified sixty-five-year-old retired Ghanaian school headmaster with silver hair, spectacles and a green-and-gold cloth shirt, tending cocoa and mango saplings in his courtyard.
Grandma Mansa: Grandpa Mensah’s warm sixty-two-year-old wife, a retired textile and foodstuff trader, wearing an amber wax-print dress and head-wrap.
Efua: their twelve-year-old granddaughter in JHS 1, curious and observant, wearing a yellow top and blue skirt.
Kojo: Efua’s thirteen-year-old brother in JHS 2, carrying a notebook and pen, wearing a green collared shirt.

narrationPlan.voice: Warm, unhurried Ghanaian storyteller (en-GH); gentle, wise cadence for Grandpa Mensah and proud clarity for Grandma Mansa.
narrationPlan.pace: Medium (about 115 words per minute); pause clearly on the Year 1 and Year 2 compounding numbers on page 5.
notes: Pronounce Efua ("eh-FOO-ah"), Kojo ("KOH-joh") and Mansa ("MAHN-sah") naturally.

music: Optional gentle acoustic guitar fingerpicking reminiscent of palm-wine highlife; off by default.
culturalNotes: Balances traditional Ghanaian respect for caring for elders with modern formal and informal-sector pension planning (SSNIT, Tier 2, Tier 3).
reviewQuestions: Is the Three-Tier Pension System explanation clear and accurate for Primary 6–JHS 2 learners?

pages.brief: Warm Ghanaian courtyard veranda filled with potted mango saplings: Grandpa Mensah (65, silver hair, spectacles, green-and-gold shirt) smiling at his phone while Grandma Mansa (amber wax-print dress) and grandchildren Efua (12, yellow top) and Kojo (13, green shirt) look on.
Grandpa Mensah standing beside a mature, shady mango tree heavy with ripe golden mangoes, gesturing from a tiny sapling pot to the giant tree as Efua and Kojo listen.
pages.narration: Wise, affectionate proverb-like metaphor linking tree planting to retirement planning.

pages.brief: At the veranda table: Grandpa Mensah opening a neat folder of old documents and drawing a simple flow of small monthly coins entering a strong vault icon (no text).
pages.narration: Clear definition of a pension and automatic monthly payroll contributions.

pages.brief: Close view at the veranda table: Efua and Kojo leaning over an open notebook with a pencil as Grandpa Mensah arranges mango seeds into groups to demonstrate compounding (no text).
pages.narration: Enthusiastic invitation to test the maths of compounding.

pages.brief: Grandpa Mensah pointing to three neat rows of mango seeds on a board: row one has ten seeds, row two adds one seed, and row three adds one seed plus an extra golden seed, while Kojo smiles in understanding.
pages.narration: Walk through the exact numbers slowly and clearly: 1,000 → 1,100 in Year 1; 10% of 1,100 = 110 → 1,210 in Year 2.

pages.brief: Grandpa Mensah holding up a sketch card showing two staircases of coins, one long green staircase starting early and rising high, and a short yellow staircase starting late (no text).
pages.narration: Emphasise the power of time and starting early.

pages.brief: Grandma Mansa smiling warmly as she places three neatly stacked colourful woven baskets on the veranda table to illustrate the Three-Tier Pension System for Efua and Kojo.
pages.narration: Warm pride from Grandma Mansa introducing the NPRA and Ghana’s Three-Tier Pension System.

pages.brief: Close view of the first two stacked baskets: beside the bottom basket sits a calendar with monthly coins (Tier 1 monthly pension); beside the second basket sits a larger tied cloth pouch (Tier 2 lump sum, no text).
pages.narration: Clear distinction between Tier 1 (SSNIT monthly pension) and Tier 2 (occupational lump-sum benefit).

pages.brief: Grandma Mansa holding the bright top basket while a visual flashback scene behind her shows her younger self at a colourful textile stall placing weekly coins into a pension passbook (no text).
pages.narration: Empowering message for informal-sector and self-employed workers in Ghana.

pages.brief: Efua raising her finger thoughtfully while Grandpa Mensah places an extra small coin pouch atop the three stacked baskets to show protection against rising prices.
pages.narration: Connects pensions back to inflation and proactive voluntary saving.

pages.brief: Golden sunlight in the courtyard: Efua and Kojo holding young mango saplings in pots while Grandpa Mensah and Grandma Mansa stand smiling beneath the big fruiting mango tree.
pages.narration: Warm, dignified conclusion blending Ghanaian family respect with lifelong financial independence.

teacherGuide.overview: An upper-primary and JHS story explaining pensions, compound growth (1,000 → 1,100 → 1,210 cedis at 10% per year), inflation awareness, and Ghana’s Three-Tier Pension System (National Pensions Act, Act 766, regulated by the NPRA: Tier 1 SSNIT monthly pension, Tier 2 mandatory lump-sum scheme, and Tier 3 voluntary personal/provident schemes including informal-sector workers).
learningGoals: Explain why workers contribute regularly to a pension during their active earning years.
Calculate two-year compound growth (1,000 cedis at 10% → 1,100 cedis in Year 1 → 1,210 cedis in Year 2) and contrast it with simple interest (1,200 cedis).
Describe the three tiers of Ghana’s pension system (Tier 1 SSNIT, Tier 2 occupational lump sum, Tier 3 voluntary/informal sector) and the role of the NPRA.
Explain why starting early and accounting for inflation matter for long-term financial security.

whileReading: Pause at the embedded comprehension and vocabulary activities to check understanding and discuss the evidence in the text.
afterReading: Simple vs Compound Growth Table: Calculate Year 1, Year 2 and Year 3 balances for 1,000 cedis at 10% under simple interest (1,100; 1,200; 1,300) versus compound growth (1,100; 1,210; 1,331).
Three-Tier Sorting Cards: Match worker profiles (a schoolteacher, a hospital nurse, a self-employed Kumasi cloth trader, a software freelancer) to how they use Tier 1, Tier 2 and Tier 3.
discussion: Why did Grandpa Mensah point to the mature mango tree when Kojo asked who was paying him in retirement?
In Year 2 of the 1,000-cedi compounding example, where did the extra 10 cedis (1,210 vs 1,200) come from?
How does Tier 3 make sure self-employed market traders, artisans, farmers and drivers in Ghana are not left out of retirement planning?
How do family care for elders and personal pension planning work together in modern Ghana?

whatWeKnow: Under Ghana’s National Pensions Act, 2008 (Act 766), the National Pensions Regulatory Authority (NPRA) regulates a Three-Tier system: Tier 1 (SSNIT mandatory basic national social security), Tier 2 (mandatory privately managed occupational scheme), and Tier 3 (voluntary provident fund and personal pension schemes designed to include informal-sector workers).
Compound growth follows the formula A = P(1 + r)^t, meaning time in the market exponentially increases the effect of reinvested returns.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Pension researchers in Ghana are studying how mobile-money micro-contributions and automated reminders can boost Tier 3 participation among informal-sector youth.

investigation.title: Year-by-Year Compounding Seed Lab
materials: 100 dried beans or maize kernels and 3 small bowls labelled "Start (Year 0)", "End of Year 1", and "End of Year 2".
steps: Count 100 beans into the Year 0 bowl (representing 1,000 cedis, where 1 bean = 10 cedis).
For Year 1 at 10% growth, add 10% of 100 beans (10 beans) to get 110 beans (1,100 cedis).
For Year 2 at 10% growth, calculate 10% of the 110 beans (11 beans) and add them to get 121 beans (1,210 cedis). Point out the 11th bean that came from Year 1’s growth!

pronunciation.guidance: three soft syllables, "eh-FOO-ah". A two-syllable "EH-fwah" is also heard in English speech.
reviewerNotes: Choose between "eh-FOO-ah" (3 syllables) and "EH-fwah" (2) for the narrator voice.
Supply IPA and mark tone if wanted.
